summary.text: Saint Constantine was the Roman emperor associated with Christianity’s legal freedom, the founding of Constantinople, and the First Ecumenical Council. His feast is shared with Saint Helena.

blocks.text: He was the son of Constantius Chlorus and Saint Helena. After his father’s death in 306, the army acclaimed him emperor at York. The OCA life situates his rise within the divided Roman imperial government.

blocks.text: The life recounts a vision of the Cross before military victory. The settlement at Milan in 313 protected Christian religious practice. In 325 he convened the Council of Nicaea, where bishops condemned Arianism and confessed the Son’s full divinity.

blocks.text: He received Baptism near the end of his life and died in 337. His burial was in Constantinople’s church of the Holy Apostles. The ecclesiastical account describes death after Baptism, not a martyr’s execution.

blocks.text: The title Equal to the Apostles identifies the Church’s commemoration of his role in supporting Christianity. His mother has a separate Saint profile; their shared feast recalls their related but distinct service to the Church.
